newsitem.title: INDIA: FUND VIEW - Threadneedle sees bulls grazing in India.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Threadneedle sees bulls grazing in India.

text.p: Indian stock markets, favoured by easing monetary conditions, will provide a grazing ground for bulls this year, especially those retreating from Southeast Asia, a senior official of ITC Threadneedle Asset Management said on Wednesday.

"We feel that a target of 4,300 for the Bombay Stock Exchange index by the end of the year should be possible," Ajay Srinivasan, chief investment officer of the Indian-British firm, told Reuters in an interview.
Bombay's benchmark 30-share index in early trading was at 3,858.21 points on Wednesday.

Falling interest rates, increased credit and foreign funds' buying, some of them switching weightings from troubled Southeast Asian emerging markets, will combine to guide Indian markets higher, he said.
"I think the real drive for the markets will come from foreign fund buying, but there will be a step-up in local interest also," Srinivasan said.
He said an easier monetary policy unveiled by India's central bank in April was a boon for stock markets.
"The Reserve Bank's credit policy for 1997/98 has thrown in a lot of liquidity. It has tilted the balance in favour of equities because debt yields have really come down," he said.
Leading banks have cut prime lending rates by 1-1.5 percentage points to 14.0-14.5 percent after the central bank's first half monetary policy unveiled on April 16.
ITC Threadneedle, equally owned by Britain's Threadneedle and India's ITC Classic Finance, operates an open-ended mutual fund.
Srinivasan said attractive valuations in Indian stocks compared with other emerging markets would lure foreign funds to Indian blue chips.
"There is a problem today in Thailand...people expect that problem to translate into Malaysia. And if there is a devaluation in Thailand, it affects Indonesia and the Philippines."
"India today doesn't have any of those negatives."
Bombay's widely tracked 30-share index rallied 48 percent from a three-year low in December to early March.
After a roller-coaster ride in 1997, the index is trading 42 percent higher over last year, but still 20 percent below its all-time record close in September 1994.
Srinivasan said he expected sagging industrial growth to pick up in coming months, but added the jury was still out.
"Typically, we would look for import growth -- which is indicative of local demand, but it's not a clear sign yet."
Several sectors of the manufacturing industry showed a slowdown in 1996/97 (April-March).
"The right signal has come from non-food credit where there is definitely growth as compared to last year."
But market analysts said it was too early to say whether industrial growth had begun an up trend.
Srinivasan said ITC Threadneedle had a strategy to buy during times of market panic.

"We look at any big panic as a good opportunity to buy, because it always distorts value. So, if there is panic and people start throwing stocks unnecessarily, like they don't want to see it again, it would be foolish not to buy them.
Srinivasan said he was bullish on refinery, pharmaceutical and software stocks. State-run Hindustan Petrochemicals Corporation Ltd (HPCL) was one of the fund's largest holdings, he said.
